attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his published newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The core claims are kept: capacity is limited, slow to build, and mostly held by the five firms. The normalised text leaves out the clause about the first three supplying Anthropic and OpenAI, but the contract puts it back as a subsidiary element. It is an unhedged present-tense observation.

contract.note: Reading 'most' as more than half, treating usable AI capacity as the main denominator, and using Q1 2026 are ordinary, fair readings. The choice of denominator (AI, hyperscale or all data-center capacity) and how overlap is counted decide the result.

evidence.note: JLL, January 2026: grid-connection lead times exceed four years in primary markets, alongside construction delays. This supports the 'take forever' and 'limited capacity' elements but says nothing about which companies hold the capacity.

Synergy, Q1 2026: Amazon, Microsoft and Google hold 57% of hyperscale capacity. Hyperscale is a different denominator from global AI capacity, and the item does not cover OpenAI's allocation or the supplier relationships.

reviews.rationale: The lead-time and constraint elements are supported. The central majority claim has no global AI-capacity inventory with allocations for all five firms. Synergy's hyperscale share is suggestive but uses a different denominator. The supplier relationships are not documented in the packet. So the evidence does not settle the claim as a whole.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his published newsletter.

semantics.note: Three observational clauses, with the hedges 'can't seem to' and 'appears to' kept. These are evidential wording about observed conditions, not probability forecasts. The 'refuses to address' clause is unhedged.

contract.note: Reading the reliability clause as recurring material disruption and the quality clause as observable regressions is fair. Counting any substantive explanation as engagement is an ordinary reading of 'refuses to discuss', though the speaker's 'actually' hints that he means adequate engagement. That reading decides clause C.

evidence.note: Official status record of a major outage across Claude.ai, the API and Claude Code on April 15, 2026, inside the window.
Contemporaneous TechRadar reporting of separate elevated-error outages on April 6 and 7. Together with e1, this shows recurring disruption.

Anthropic's postmortem shows a Claude Code prompt change shipped April 16 that cut quality on an evaluation. It was published later but documents a defect from before publication. It supports a specific product regression.
On April 12, before the article, Cherny publicly explained the reasoning-default change and its rationale. That is substantive engagement, which contradicts a refusal to discuss.

reviews.rationale: Clause A holds: outages are documented on April 6, 7 and 15. Clause B holds: the postmortem shows a regression introduced April 16. Clause C fails: Anthropic staff publicly explained the disputed changes before publication, and the article itself quotes a Cherny response. Two clauses are supported and one is contradicted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: A firm counterfactual conditional ('would quickly fall apart') with its antecedent kept. The aside about API profitability is rightly left out as a separate opinion.

contract.note: Requiring a verified forced move to cost-covering prices before scoring is faithful to the antecedent. 'Actual costs', 'forced' and 'quickly' are undefined, so interpretation would decide any result.

evidence.note: Report of Anthropic's April 2026 move to usage-based enterprise billing. It does not show forced pricing or prices that cover actual costs, so the antecedent is not met.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent, Anthropic being forced to charge its actual costs, is not shown to have happened. Metered billing alone does not establish it. Under policy, a conditional whose antecedent did not occur or is unknown is not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own causal assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Faithfully states the causal split: shortfalls come from serving customers, not from being unable to serve them, and customers alone bear the cost of the capacity limits. It covers both Anthropic and OpenAI.

contract.note: The plain reading, which includes lost business as company harm, fits the speaker's point that capacity limits do not cost the companies. 'Financial shortfall' and 'paying the price' are undefined, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: OpenAI's CFO says more compute would have sped up monetization. This is management belief about 2023–2025, not a measured loss in the target period, so it is context only.
Shows customer-facing disruption on April 15. It does not show capacity as the cause or that customers alone bore the cost.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no breakdown of service costs and revenue, and no measured company-side losses from capacity limits, for either firm in January to April 2026. The OpenAI CFO statement challenges the claim's logic but is an earlier-period belief. The causal claim cannot be settled on this evidence.
